newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac earns low marks for meet-the-young TV show.
newsitem.headline: Chirac earns low marks for meet-the-young TV show.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac earned mostly poor marks in the French press on Tuesday for his televised turn before young people, and pledges to give schools computers, eradicate illiteracy and boost youth employment.
The conservative Le Figaro said the Gaullist president, in his two-hour television interview on Monday night, had chosen the role of a friendly president-big brother to the younger generation.

"He has shown that he knows his subject: he tried to twist the neck of general gloom. He won't succeed in just a few weeks, but there is something reassuring in his obstinacy and good humour," the paper said in an editorial.
In his interview, Chirac also sought to encourage firms to hire young people hard hit by unemployment and pledged better adult re-training to help people switch careers.

Other newspapers were less kind. "Chirac: Much Ado About Nothing," headlined the Communist Party daily L'Humanite, which denounced what it called a flurry of platitudes and mini-proposals a million years away from people's expectations.

"For the young, finding out that their school is going to be plugged onto Internet is perhaps not their first concern," echoed opposition Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande in an interview on RTL radio.
"People were awaiting action on jobs today, not on prospects after the year 2,000. People are disappointed," Hollande said.

Jean-Francois Mancel, spokesman for Chirac's RPR party, retorted that he had been impassioned and fascinating, and had answered all the expectations of young people hit by a 25 percent unemployment rate which is double the national average.

But the left-leaning Liberation said the head of state had stage-managed the programme on the eve of a tour of Latin America simply to hog the limelight and avert any accusations that this was no time to travel abroad.
"Unemployment statistics could prompt one to think that jobs for parents are just as much of an emergency as jobs for their children," Liberation said in an editorial.
"In any case, it seems more and more difficult to assure young people that they will soon start a career...On that issue, (Chirac) was unsatisfactory," it said.

Chirac, speaking from Paris's Science City against a backdrop of a gleaming geodesic dome, said he wanted all secondary schools to be connected to the Internet by the year 2000 to develop computer skills and improve job prospects linked to information technology.
He also said that he wanted to eradicate illiteracy for children entering high school by the end of his seven-year mandate in the year 2002.

"A great nation is one that knows how to integrate all its children," he told France 2 television in the broadcast that echoed a drive by U.S. President Bill Clinton to computerise U.S. schools and combat illiteracy.
Chirac said he had asked the government to cut value added tax on multimedia products and services, including CD-ROMs, to the lowest rate of 5.6 percent from 20.6 percent.

In contrast to the last major television interview he gave in December, in which he blamed the French people's innate conservatism for economic stagnation, Chirac sought to project optimism about France's dynamism.
He also urged companies to do more to hire young people, accusing them of focusing too narrowly on profits.

An opinion poll published by the Journal du Dimanche newspaper showed young people had more confidence in themselves (65 percent) or their parents (40 percent) than in the president (13 percent) to "prepare their future and that of our society".
